title: Tamsin and the Bridge
premise: In 1919, in a river town scarred by occupation and armistice negotiations, Rafael 'Tamsin' Oyelaran — an apprentice clockmaker who survived the war years by being useful and invisible — is summoned to repair the observatory's master clock. Hidden inside its case she finds a ledger bearing every name the occupying army conscripted, deported, or erased, including her own dead brother's. When the army returns to requisition the town and seize all records, Tamsin must smuggle the ledger past three checkpoints with the help of a found family of bridge-keepers, nuns, and deserters, before the armistice delegation signs — or walks away. She reaches the delegation in time, at the cost of the clock itself and nearly her own life, and the names are read aloud into the record; in the end she chooses to stay, rebuild the clock, and let the town's survivors become her family.
about_author: Zephyrine Galloway is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing requisition records from occupied European towns. She writes historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Clock That Kept Wrong Time
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Summoned to the hilltop observatory, she diagnoses the master clock's failure and discovers a hidden compartment containing a ledger of names. The emotional beat is wary curiosity hardening into dread as she recognizes her brother's name among the erased.

chapters.title: What the River Keeps
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She descends to the bridge district where she lives among the found family who took her in after the war: old Marta the bridge-keeper, Brother Anselm, and deserter Kolya. She hides the ledger beneath the toll house floorboards. Beat: belonging, and the fear of endangering it.

chapters.title: Requisition
chapters.summary: Kolya's POV. Soldiers arrive to requisition the town, its grain, and every official record; the observatory archive is sealed. Tamsin realizes the ledger is now the only copy of the truth. Beat: the fragile peace shattering, and quiet resolve replacing fear.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Studying the checkpoints — the bridge, the customs house, the delegation's perimeter — she maps a route with Marta and Kolya. A soldier she once repaired a watch for patrols the bridge. Beat: planning as an act of hope, shadowed by the cost if caught.

chapters.title: The Toll House Burns
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. A reprisal fire destroys the toll house and nearly the hidden ledger; Marta saves it but is arrested on suspicion. Beat: grief and guilt — survival has a price, and someone else paid this installment.

chapters.title: A Watch for Sergeant Brandt
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. To free Marta, Tamsin approaches Sergeant Brandt under the pretense of repairing his dead son's watch, trading small truths for information about the armistice timetable. Beat: dangerous intimacy; using usefulness as armor one last time.

chapters.title: Crossing at Low Water
chapters.summary: Kolya's POV. The first two checkpoints fall to misdirection — a funeral procession, a bribed ferryman — but Kolya is wounded covering Tamsin's escape through the customs house. Beat: the found family holding together under fire, each sacrifice deepening the stakes.

chapters.title: The Armistice That Isn't
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. News breaks that the delegation may withdraw without signing, which would void any testimony. Trapped outside the perimeter with a wounded friend and a night left, Tamsin must choose between waiting safely and forcing entry. Beat: despair transfigured into defiance.

chapters.title: Every Name Aloud
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Climax. She enters the observatory through the clock tower she knows better than anyone, interrupts the signing with the ledger, and reads the names until the delegates accept them into the record. Brandt lets her pass; the army seizes the master clock instead. Beat: triumph purchased with exposure — she can no longer be invisible.

chapters.title: Tamsin and the Bridge
chapters.summary: Marta's POV, weeks later. Marta released, Kolya mending, the town rebuilding around the emptied tower. Tamsin begins building a new clock whose chimes will sound the names once a year. Beat: resolution — inheritance reclaimed not as property but as memory, and family chosen, kept, and home.
